analysis.one_liner: Lets student loans be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote; student loans remain largely non-dischargeable in bankruptcy.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1976, Congress has carved student loans out of normal bankruptcy rules, so borrowers can only erase them by proving 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that most people cannot meet it [S3]. This bill would delete that carve-out entirely, letting a person in bankruptcy treat government, nonprofit, and private student loans the same as credit card debt or medical bills [S2][S3]. A Republican from Wisconsin introduced it with one Democratic cosponsor, and it never moved [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers who fall into genuine financial distress — people with disabilities, job losses, or medical catastrophes — would regain a normal way out, instead of fighting a lawsuit to prove 'undue hardship'. Future borrowers would benefit indirectly, since lenders facing the risk of discharge would have an incentive to price loans and lend responsibly.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the special rule (11 U.S.C. §523(a)(8)) that makes student loans non-dischargeable, so they can be erased in bankruptcy like most other debts.
Covers government, nonprofit, and private student loans, plus obligations to repay scholarships, stipends, or educational benefits.
Applies only to debts taken out after enactment, so it does not retroactively change existing loans.

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders and loan servicers, who currently hold debts that borrowers cannot walk away from. The federal government also bears the cost as a creditor when its loans are discharged, and lenders would likely charge future students somewhat higher rates to cover the added risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student lenders and the federal government

drawbacks.text: Removing discharge protection raises the risk to lenders, which would likely mean higher interest rates or tighter lending for future students, including low-income students who borrow most.
Discharged federal loans are a cost to taxpayers, since the Department of Education is the creditor on most student debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: distressed borrowers get a real exit from unpayable debt, and the cost is somewhat higher borrowing costs for future students plus losses to the federal loan portfolio. Roughly two-thirds of bankruptcy filers with student debt already seek to discharge other debts, so the change mainly restores a safety valve that existed for most of American history. The bill is a clean two-page deletion of the carve-out with no income limits or waiting periods, which favors borrowers broadly but gives Congress no graduated approach.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Introduced July 20, 2021 by Rep. Glenn Grothman (R-WI) and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
On November 1, 2022, more than a year later, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where it remained.
The bill ended the 117th Congress without any further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever held.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders, servicers, and the Department of Education as a creditor are better off, because student loans remain the only major consumer debt most borrowers cannot erase in bankruptcy.

sides.party_line_note: A conservative Republican sponsored the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, so the fight never became a party-line vote — it died in committee before any vote could test broader support.

industries.note: These companies hold loans that borrowers currently cannot discharge, a collection guarantee other consumer lenders do not enjoy. The bill would end that guarantee, so the industry's interest in keeping the status quo runs against distressed borrowers seeking relief.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program (Department of Education as creditor)
industries.note: The federal government is the creditor on most student debt and would absorb losses from discharges. But it also lends to the same borrowers the bill would help, so its role as creditor and as the public's lender pulls in both directions.
